chunks: "I'd read asymmetrical half-bridge two ways, and the answer is similar for both.
One is a half-bridge whose two FETs are deliberately different: the high-side and low-side have different on-resistance and gate charge.
The other is a half-bridge driving a one-way load, where the output only ever swings between zero and the supply.
You can use that whenever the load only needs one polarity and the duty cycle is lopsided. A buck converter stepping 12 volts down to 1.
2 volts is on for 10% of the time, so the low-side FET carries the current 90% of the time.
If I split the same silicon area so the low side is three times more conductive than the high side, I cut conduction loss by about 20%.
Solenoids, fans, heaters and LEDs are the same story: they need one polarity, so one leg is enough.

I need a symmetrical H-bridge when the load needs both polarities with equal strength: a motor that reverses and brakes, a voice coil, a class-D amplifier driving a speaker, or a transformer that needs zero DC volt-seconds.
There the duty cycle averages around 50% and both directions carry the same current, so equal FETs are the right choice, and a single leg can't make a negative voltage anyway."
